Microaerated UASB reactor treating textile wastewater: The core
microbiome and removal of azo dye Direct Black 22

h i g h l i g h t s
 Microaeration in UASB reactor promoted complete removal of azo dye Direct Black 22.
 Similar COD and sulfate removal for anaerobic and microaerated UASB reactors.
 Efﬂuent toxicity was removed after microaeration.
 Putative aromatic amines degraders microbes developed in the microaerobic zone.

a b s t r a c t
Sequential anaerobic and aerobic processes have been recommended to treat textile wastewater reliably.
In this work, the focus was on ﬁnding an energetically more competitive system to remove tetra-azo dye
Direct Black 22 (DB22). We operated two upﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactors (R1 and R2) in
three phases (PI, PII, and PIII). R1 was operated as a conventional UASB, while R2 was microaerated in the
upper part (0.18 ± 0.05 mg O2. L1), aiming to remove DB22 simultaneously with the aromatic amine
byproducts. PI consisted of feeding reactors with synthetic textile wastewater (STW), PII had higher
salinity in the STW, and PIII was the same as PII, plus sulfate. The results showed that color and COD
removal efﬁciencies were similar for both reactors (67e72% for R1 and 59e78% for R2) without a sub-
stantial inﬂuence of oxygen in R2. However, microaeration played a crucial role in R2 by removing the
anaerobically formed aromatic amines; during PIII, the efﬂuent was 16 times less toxic than that of R1.
The microbial community that developed in the sludge bed of both reactors was quite similar, with the
core microbiome represented by Trichococcus, Syntrophus and Methanosaeta genera. The increase in
salinity in PII and PIII promoted a shift in the microbial community, excluding salty-sensitive genera from
the core microbiome. The putative genera Brevundimonas and Ornatilinea were associated to aromatic
amine microaerobic removal. Therefore, there is a potential application of a compact microaerated
anaerobic system for textile wastewater treatment.

1. Introduction
Textile and apparel industries are a signiﬁcant sector of the
national economy in low-middle income countries (GNI < $12,055
e The World Bank, 2017). The faster this industrial sector grows, the
faster the environmental issues spread due to the resulting
pollution of its activities. Global clothing production has been
developed mainly in Bangladesh, India, Korea, Cambodia, Brazil and
Pakistan (Tewari, 2005), and China, which alone is responsible for
32% of the textile fabrics and production of ready-made garments
in the world (AEPC, 2018). Unskilled workers and poor infrastruc-
ture are still common features of the textile industries in most of
those countries. Additionally, the lack of regulation associated with
the use of a huge variety of dyes and chemicals contribute to
increased pollution, making it difﬁcult to standardize treatment
processes for textile wastewater.

Synthetic dyes are industrially preferred over natural dyes due
to their high ﬁxation properties. The dyes mostly used in industries,
such as textile, cosmetics, and paper printing, are synthetic azo
dyes corresponding approximately to 70% of the total dyes used by
these industries (Stick and Mocerino, 2009). During the dyebath in
textile industries, ﬁxation to fabrics is usually incomplete, resulting
in wastewater very rich in dyes. An advantageous eco-friendly and
low-cost treatment alternative is the use of two-step biological
processes. The ﬁrst step consists of an anaerobic phase in which the
azo bonds are cleaved by azoreductase enzymes, resulting in
colorless wastewater, although full of toxic byproducts (aromatic
amines) (Field et al.,1995; Weisburger, 2002). A further aerobic step
is required to achieve the bioconversion or complete removal of the
aromatic amines (Van Der Zee and Villaverde, 2005; Bonakdarpour
et al., 2011; Khan et al., 2014; Sandhya et al., 2005).
Sequencing batch reactors (SBR) and bioﬁlm electrode reactors
(BER), operating under microaerobic or anaerobic-aerobic condi-
tions, have efﬁciently been used for textile wastewater treatment at
the bench scale, removing from 70% to 90% of COD and color,
respectively (Cao et al., 2018; Çinar et al., 2008; Srinivasan and
Sadasivam, 2018). However, although promising reactor setups,
they have not been sufﬁciently tested on a real scale. Additionally,
those reactor conﬁgurations demand skilled operators due to the
high level of automation applied and frequent maintenance re-
quirements, thus hampering their application for many small and
moderately sized industries. In contrast, the UASB reactor type is
well known for its easy handling and low operational costs
(Lettinga and Pol, 1991); comparatively, it also has high efﬁciency
for azo dye decolorization (Patel, 2015). UASB has also shown good
efﬁciency in real textile wastewater treatment in a pilot-scale
reactor (Amaral et al., 2014). However, the efﬂuent still demands
an aerobic post-treatment to guarantee aromatic amine removal
and, consequently, remove wastewater toxicity.
Therefore, in this work, a novel approach system to treat textile
wastewater was evaluated using microaeration in a conventional
UASB. The aim was to create two different redox zones: an anaer-
obic zone deeper in the sludge bed and a microaerobic zone from
the middle to the upper part of the reactor. The complete degra-
dation of azo dyes in a single treatment unit was the main target of
the approach. We also investigated the effects of microaeration,
salinity, and sulfate on the structure of the microbial community.
The performance of the reactor was based on the chemical oxygen
demand (COD) and color removal efﬁciency, as well as the resulting
efﬂuent toxicity.
2. Experimental procedures
We operated two identical UASB acrylic reactors (R1 and R2 e
Fig. 1) with a 6 L working volume (12 cm diameter and 60 cm
height) under mesophilic temperature (25.0 ± 1.4 C). Sampling
ports were placed at 4 (S4), 14 (S14), and 24 cm (S24) from the
bottom of the reactors. R1 was a traditional UASB reactor and
operated as a control. R2 was partially microaerated by an air
diffuser placed 25 cm from the bottom and supplied by an aquar-
ium pump (Boyu®, U-2800, China). The dissolved oxygen (DO) was
kept at 0.18 ± 0.05 mg O2 L1 at sampling port S24.
We fed the reactors with synthetic textile wastewater (STW),
which was refrigerated (7 ± 1 C) and pumped (model 323, Watson
Marlow®, United Kingdom) to the reactors, passing through a
water bath (40 ± 5 C) (NI1225, Nova Instruments®, Brazil). The
mesophilic reactor temperature range was maintained using a
heating jacket (thermal blanket, Etaﬂon®, Brazil). Both reactors
were inoculated with anaerobic sludge (2.62 g STV L1 in the mixed
liquor) from a pilot-scale UASB reactor that was previously used to
treat real textile wastewater (Amaral et al., 2014).
We conducted the experiment for over 290 days divided into
three operational phases (P). At phase PI (150 days the STW con-
tained natural salinity of 1.9 g NaCl L1, while at phase PII (100 days)
sodium chloride was added to STW to reach salinity of 2.9 g NaCl
L1, and at PIII (40 days) salinity was maintained, as in PII, plus extra
sulfate of 250 mg SO42 L1.
2.1. Synthetic textile wastewater (STW)
The STW was based on a real textile wastewater composition, as
described by Amorim et al. (2013). It was prepared using 0.06 mM
of the tetra-azo dye Direct Black 22 (DB22, C44H32N13Na3O11S3; C. I.
35435; CAS 6473-13-8; molecular weight of 1083.97 g mol1);
starch (1200 mg O2 L1 as COD); and macro and micronutrient
solutions (Florencio et al., 1993). The dye was prehydrolyzed before
use by adjusting the pH to 11.0 ± 0.05 using NaOH (20% w:w), fol-
lowed by 1 h heating at 80 C and a ﬁnal pH readjustment to
7.0 ± 0.05 at room temperature using HCl (37%). We prepared the
starch solution using commercial corn starch (Maizena®, Brazil)
and tap water by stirring at 90 C for 30 min.
2.2. Reactor monitoring
The reactors were monitored based on the following parame-
ters: ﬂow rate, pH, temperature, and DO (daily); color, chemical
oxygen demand (COD), oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), alka-
linity, and sulfate (3 times a week); and sulﬁde (2 times a week).
The analytical methods followed the Standard Methods for the Ex-
amination of Water and Wastewater (APHA, 1998). The aromatic
amine formation was qualitatively evaluated through spectropho-
tometric light scanning at the range of 200e350 nm wavelength, as
recommended by Pinheiro et al. (2004), using ﬁltered samples
(ﬁberglass membrane 0.45 mm, Sartorius®, Germany).
2.3. Toxicity analysis
The assays were performed using Vibrio ﬁscheri as a toxicity
indicator microorganism following the protocols of Microtox®

and (B) microaerated UASB - R2.
J.R.S. Carvalho et al. / Chemosphere 242 (2020) 125157

(Microtox Model 500 analyzer, Strategic Diagnostics, Inc. SDIX,
Newark-DE, USA). We monitored cell luminescence inhibition
during 30 min. The results were expressed as the dilution factor
(DF) required for the efﬂuent not to cause toxic effects on Vibrio
ﬁscheri.
2.4. Identiﬁcation of the microbial community
We collected eight biomass samples for DNA extraction: inoc-
ulum (sample 1); sludge bed of R1 at the end of each operational
phase (sample 2 e PI; sample 3 e PII; and sample 4 e PIII); sludge
bed of R2 at the end of each operational phase (sample 5 e PI;
sample 6 e PII; and sample 7 e PIII); and sludge attached to the air
diffuser in R2 at the end of PIII (sample 8). We used a Power Kit
Soil® (MO Bio laboratories, Carlsbad-CA, USA) for DNA extraction
according to the manufacturer’s protocols. DNA quantiﬁcation was
carried out using a NanoDrop2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo
Scientiﬁc, USA). The DNA was stored at 20 C and was subjected to
amplicon sequencing (bTEFAP®, USA) using Illumina MiSeq.
Sequencing was performed by Mr. DNA Molecular Research LP
(Shallowater-TX, USA) using the universal primer 515 F paired with
907R for both domains, Achaea and Bacteria, with 20,000 reads and
2  300 bp. The pipeline used followed the MiSeq manufacturer’s
guidelines. Sequences were aligned and depleted of barcodes. Then,
sequences with less than 150 bp were discarded, as well as se-
quences with ambiguous base calls. We clustered the sequences
and removed the chimeras. Operational taxonomic units (OTUs)
were deﬁned by clustering at 3% divergence (97% similarity). Final
OTUs were taxonomically classiﬁed using BLASTn against a curated
database derived from RDPII and NCBI platforms (www.ncbi.nlm.
nih.gov, http://rdp.cme.msu.edu). We deposited the sequencing
data yielded in this study in the European Nucleotide Archive under
the accession number PRJEB33520.
2.5. Statistical analysis
Statistical Analysis of Metagenomic Proﬁles (STAMP) (Parks
et al., 2014) was the software used to identify the signiﬁcant
changes in community structure that resulted from salinity and
sulfate concentration additions over the operational phases. When
the p-value was lower than 0.05, the differences were considered
statistically signiﬁcant.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. COD and color removal
The organic loading rate (OLR) ranged from 1.27 to 1.50 kg COD
m3 d1 during the entire operational period. The performance of
both reactors concerning the COD removal was similar for each
operational phase (Table 1). In PI, the removal efﬁciencies for R1
and R2 were 72 ± 17% and 78 ± 18%, respectively; in PII, 67 ± 10%
and 59 ± 10%; and in PIII, 69 ± 6% and 70 ± 8%. These results show
ﬁrst that the oxygen supplied to R2 did not enhance the removal
efﬁciency (p > 0.05). Second, by increasing the salinity level from
1.9 (PI) to 2.9 g of NaCl L1 (PII), we observed a decrease in the
removal efﬁciency for both reactors. However, in the case of R1, the
difference was not statistically signiﬁcant (p 0.6), while for R2, the
removal efﬁciency dropped from 78% (PI) to 59% (PII) (p ¼ 0.001).
Third, recovery was observed from PII to PIII in both reactors, but
especially for R2 (from 59% to 70%); this can be an indication of
microbial adaptation to the higher salinity level associated with the
sulfate added, applied in PIII. In PII, the drop in COD removal efﬁ-
ciencies observed for both reactors can be attributed to the changes
in the microbial community (data shown on item 3.4), which was
affected by the higher salinity compared to that of PI.
The recovered COD removal efﬁciency in PIII might be related to
sulfate addition because sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) use elec-
trons from the organic matter more efﬁciently than methanogens
due to the thermodynamic advantage (Muyzer and Stams, 2008),
competing mainly by propionate and butyrate.
Concerning the color removal, the performance was also similar
for both reactors in the ﬁrst two phases. In PI, the removal efﬁciency
was 78 ± 10% for R1 and 80 ± 12% for R2. In PII, the values were
slightly lower, 73 ± 17% for R1 and 71 ± 11% for R2. Comparing these
results with those of COD removal, there is a noticeable difference
in the salinity inﬂuence on the microorganisms. The higher salinity
in PII compared to that in PI resulted in a decrease of color and COD
removal efﬁciencies, especially for R2. However, in the case of color
removal, the R2 efﬁciency decreased by only 9%, while that of COD
removal was 19%. One explanation is that dye-degrading microor-
ganisms are less sensitive than those of COD.
The inﬂuence of the added sulfate on PIII color removal efﬁ-
ciency (69% ± 9% for R1 and 69 ± 11% for R2) was not signiﬁcant
when comparing the results of both reactors (p ¼ 0.97). Color
removal may either be stimulated or suppressed by sulfate because
it competes with azo dyes for the electrons available, and sulﬁde
also stimulates dye chemical removal (Prato-Garcia et al., 2013).
Simultaneous sulfate and azo dye reduction are also supported by
the ORP, which was e 300 ± 86 mV in the sludge bed of both re-
actors during PIII (S4, Fig. 2). Lourenço et al. (2001) reported that
color removal efﬁciency increased with lower ORP values. Sulfate
reduction occurs when ORP is approximately 220 mV, consid-
ering SO42 degradation over H2S formation (Yoo et al., 2001),
whereas azo dye reduction is reported to occur in the range
from 50 mV to 600 mV depending on the type of azo dye (Dos
Santos et al., 2004; Rau and Stolz, 2003).
3.2. Sulfate removal
In PIII, the sulfate removal efﬁciency was 60 ± 10% and 36 ± 17%
for R1 and R2, respectively (Fig. 2). The low R2 efﬁciency can be
attributed to the microaeration supplying the futile sulfur cycle. In
the bottom part of R2, the inﬂuent sulfate was anaerobically con-
verted to sulﬁde, which was partially reconverted to sulfate under
oxygen exposure in the upper part. The ORP proﬁle indicated that
anaerobic conditions were established across the whole R1 height
(ORP from 296 to 368 mV - Fig. 2A), while typical microaerobic
ORP was detected in R2 at the height S24 (56.7 ± 22 mV) and at
the
outlet
(95.1 ± 50 mV).
Thus,
favorable
conditions
were
conﬁrmed in R2 for the sulfur futile cycle establishment. From a
microbiological perspective, the sulfate removal efﬁciency decrease
in R2 can also be attributed to the high sensitivity of SRB microbes
to molecular oxygen as they are strictly anaerobes. Oxygen in-
activates various enzymes of SRB when exposed under long periods
(Fukui, 2002; Krekeler et al., 1998).

3.3. Aromatic amines
We detected aromatic amines in the efﬂuent of both reactors
only after the ﬁrst 30 days of operation (data not shown). Their
removal was observed only in the microaerated R2 from day 148
onwards. In R1 during the entire experiment, the formed aromatic
amines were not removed, and they were always detected in all
three sampling points and the reactor efﬂuent (Fig. 3). In R2, the
aromatic amines that formed in the anaerobic zone, detected at
sampling points S4 and S14, were partially removed from R2
efﬂuent (Fig. 3).
Concerning the toxicity on Vibrio ﬁscheri, two factors were
considered in the STW, the azo dye itself and the salinity. The acute
toxicity endpoint is the effective concentration of a chemical that
causes a 50% reduction in the bioluminescence of the bacteria. We
did not identify signiﬁcant acute toxicity in the azo dye DB22-
containing STW (Table 2), as also reported by Menezes et al.

(2019). Low permeability of azo dye for cells due to the presence of
sulfonated groups in the DB22 molecular structure may be
responsible for the absence of acute toxicity. In the case of the
salinity addition effect, the STW dilution factor increased from 1
(PI) to 2 (PII and PIII), indicating salt toxicity against Vibrio ﬁscheri,
which is known to be affected by salinity (Cook et al., 2000). In the
R1 efﬂuent, aromatic amines were associated with an increased and
strong toxicity level, as shown by a dilution factor of 14 and 16,
measured at the end of PII and PIII, respectively. On the other hand,
in the R2 efﬂuent, the aromatic amines were removed or converted
into nontoxic compounds, resulting in the absence of acute toxicity.
Therefore, these results provide evidence of the microaeration role
on aromatic amines removal, complementing the anaerobic pro-
cess for azo dyes removal.
3.4. Microbial community
The most abundant phyla in the sludge bed samples from both
reactors and their respective relative abundance (RA) range during
the experiment were Proteobacteria (13.17e44.21%), Firmicutes
(7.12e41.94%),
Bacteroidetes
(13.05e26.17%),
and
Chloroﬂexi
(2.51e4.77%). These phyla are commonly found in the microbial
community of anaerobic systems, usually with RA above 1%
(K€ochling et al., 2017; Okada et al., 2013).
Thirty-six OTUs were identiﬁed in R1 sludge bed samples at the
genus level (with RA> 1% at least in one of the phases), of which 17
were prevalent with RA higher than 0.1% during the entire exper-
iment (Fig. 4). In the case of R2 samples, we identiﬁed a total of 31
OTUs, of which 15 were also considered to be of high prevalence
(RA>1%).
In this work, the COD removal in both reactors (Table 1) was
supported by the core microbiome related to carbon cycling
because it was composed of the fermentative bacterial genera of
Trichococcus, Bacteroides, Clostridium, and Fusobacterium, meth-
anogenic archaea genera of Methanosaeta and Methanobacterium,
and an important syntrophic bacterial genus, i.e., Syntrophus. The
latter is responsible for metabolic linking of fermentative and
methanogenic microbes. Syntrophic
interactions
can
support
anaerobic digestion from organic compounds to methane (Jackson
et al., 1999). The syntrophic chain was well established over the
operational phases in R1 and R2 with increasing RA of the
fermentative Trichococcus, from less than 1% and 2.45% in PI to
7.51% and 16% in PII and to 11.58% and 34.58% in PIII, respectively.
This genus might have used starch as a substrate to produce ace-
tate, formate, and ethanol. Following the chain, the strict anaerobe
Syntrophus also exhibited increasing RA from PI (<1% in R1 and R2)
to PIII (4.27% in R1 and 3.29% in R2). These species are known as
oxidizers of volatile fatty acids, benzoate, and crotonate to acetate
in the presence of H2/formate-utilizing methanogens (Kuever,
2014;
Jackson
et
al., 1999).
The
occurrence
of
the
Meth-
anobacterium genus, a H2/formate-utilizing archaea, supported
Syntrophus activity. Finally, acetate was converted to methane by
Methanosaeta, where RA reached 8.50% and 2.61% in PIII, for R1 and
R2, respectively. The lower RA found in R2 compared to R1 can be
explained by the possible oxygen sensitivity of some methanogens
(Kiener and Leisinger, 1983; Patell and Sprott, 1990). Menezes et al.
(2019) detected a 50% inhibition of the methane production rate
when operating a batch reactor with intermittent microaeration
and similar wastewater composition, except for sulfate and salinity.
The coexistence of many other metabolisms in the core micro-
biome was due to the wastewater composition because aromatic
(Pseudomonas, Flavobacterium, and Sphingobacterium) and sulfate-
reducing microbes (Desulfobulbus, Desulfovibrio), for instance,
were also identiﬁed. All these genera play a key role during the
treatment of textile wastewater.
The main sulfate-reducing bacterial (SRB) genera identiﬁed in
the microbial community from both reactors were Desulfobulbus,
Desulfomicrobium, Desulfotomaculum, and Desulfovibrio. In R1, the
RA of all SRB species increased over the operational phases, cor-
responding to 4.07% (PI), 6.33% (PII) and 8.91% (PIII). In R2 however,
the RA of all SRB species slightly decreased (5.64% in PI, 3.46% in PII,
and 3.78% in PIII), which supports the hypothesis that microaera-
tion affected SRB development.
The beta diversity of the OTUs was analyzed using the Bray-
Curtis index (Fig. 5). We observed the ﬁrst shift in the microbial
community by comparing the microbiome identiﬁed in the

inoculum (day 1 of operation) and the microbiome identiﬁed at the
end of PI (day 150 of operation). In that case, R1 and R2 were 87%
phylogenetically divergent from the inoculum (Fig. 5). However, the
diversity among R1 and R2 in PI was quite similar (48% similarity,
Fig. 5). The microaeration in R2 stimulated the growth of facultative
anaerobic genera such as Pseudomonas (RA 10.83%) and Clostridium
(RA 8.79%), while in R1, the presence of obligate anaerobic genera
was widely observed, with Fusobacterium being the most abundant
genus identiﬁed in PI (RA 18.62%). Despite the difference in taxo-
nomic structure, a similar metabolic behavior is inferred for the
microbial communities of both reactors.
Another important factor is that the ﬁrst shift in PI was driven by
the difference in the composition of the wastewater that was
feeding reactors and sludges. The STW used to feed the reactors
contained starch and only one type of azo dye, while the real textile
wastewater to which the inoculum was previously exposed con-
tained a mixture of dyes, high sulfate concentration, and many
chemical compounds as described by Amaral et al. (2017). The
genera
Kosmotoga,
Synergistes,
Actinomyces
and
Caldisericum
related to the reduction of sulfur-complexed metals and thiosulfate
were identiﬁed with RA>1% in the inoculum sample. However, at
the end of PI, these genera were not signiﬁcant in the core micro-
biome, presenting RA close to 0% during the rest of the experiment.
The salt increase in PII caused the second shift, clustering R1 and
R2 with an even closer index of diversity (72% similarity), high-
lighting the strong inﬂuence of salinity on the microbes’ selection
(higher salinity, Fig. 5). The species Sulfuricurvum kujiense was
washed out from both reactors due to the salinity increase, even
with the availability of its preferable substrates, with RA dropping
from 7.49 (PI) to 0.18% (PII) in R1 and from 4.76 (PI) to 0.09% (PII) in
R2. This sulfur-oxidizing bacterium utilizes sulﬁde, elemental sul-
fur, thiosulfate and hydrogen as electron donors under micro-
aerobic or anaerobic conditions, but it is very sensitive to salinity
(Han et al., 2012; Kodama and Watanabe, 2004). On the other hand,
some genera endowed with high salinity resistance took the op-
portunity to increase their dominance in the microbial community.
For example, in R2, Trichococcus pasteurii, a microbial species
associated with carbon removal, exhibited an RA 6.5 times higher in
PII (15.86%) and 14 times in PIII (34.58%) than in PI (2.43%). Similar
behavior was found for this species in R1, but with lower RA. Sulfate
addition in PIII did not cause any signiﬁcant shift in the microbial
beta diversity (Fig. 5).
An important aspect concerning the beta diversity index anal-
ysis is related to the microbial community that developed attached
to the aerator, which presented only 17% similarity compared with
the sludge bed samples. The microorganisms in the reactor zone
near the air diffuser, located 25 cm from the reactor bottom, were
exposed to oxygen and dye degradation byproducts (i.e. aromatic
amines). Therefore, microaerating the intermediate zone of the
UASB reactor promoted aromatic amine degradation during PII and
PIII. Concerning the developed microbial community, species of the
genus Brevundimonas were found in the aerator biomass in PIII at
an RA of 2.65%. An important highlight related to the Brevundi-
monas genus is that the highest RA in the sludge bed samples of R2,
during PI, was 0.26%, while that in R1 was only approximately
0.04%. This genus was studied by Konopka et al. (1989), who
identiﬁed the ability of some species to mineralize aniline via meta-
cleavage of the aromatic ring induced by the catechol 2,3 oxygenase
enzyme. We identiﬁed some other genera related to the degrada-
tion of aromatic compounds in the biomass collected in the
microaerated zone. The genus Ornatilinea was identiﬁed with RA of
13.47% in the aerator sample, higher than the RA identiﬁed in the
sludge bed samples (1.14e2.61%). The fermentative genus Ornati-
linea is classiﬁed within the family Anaerolineaceae, which has been
commonly identiﬁed in mixed cultures of anaerobic reactors, as
putative aromatic degrader microorganisms (Kümmel et al., 2015;
Zhang et al., 2017; Rosenkranz et al., 2013). Sun et al. (2015),
identiﬁed a bacterial phylotype within the family Anaerolineaceae,
demonstrating the capability to assimilate aniline, an aromatic
amine potentially formed after azo dye breakdown. The literature
has shown important ﬁndings about the putative genera Bre-
vundimonas
and
members
from
the
family
Anaerolineaceae.
Nevertheless, further investigation of their enzymatic capabilities is
required to expand the current knowledge about these genera in
aromatic amines degradation.

4. Conclusions
Microaerating the upper part of a UASB reactor favored the
degradation of the tetra-azo dye Direct Black 22. Aromatic amines
formed in the lower anaerobic zone were partially removed in the
upper microaerobic zone. A large variety of genera able to perform
the complete anaerobic digestion of organic matter, while simul-
taneously removing dye and reducing sulfate were present in the
microbial community. The sludge bed core microbiome of both
reactors was quite similar, represented by Trichococcus, Syntrophus,
and Methanosaeta. Changes in the salinity level and sulfate con-
centration in the synthetic textile wastewater modiﬁed the mi-
crobial community structure. However, after adaptation, COD and
color removal efﬁciencies remained high, within the range of
59e78% and 69e79%, respectively, during the operational period.
The sulfate removal efﬁciency in the microaerated UASB reactor
diminished during the last operational phase (PIII), dropping from
53% to 36%, reﬂecting oxygen inﬂuence on SRB development. The
aromatic amines removal through microaeration produced an
efﬂuent free of toxicity, thus conﬁrming its great potential
application.
